# Pallium: telling look-alikes apart {#sec-pallium}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="2.2"></div>

Since the association stage the animal learns from pain which bushes to avoid. It learns that on the look of a
bush, a handful of colour features, by strengthening the synapses from those features onto its aversive cells.
That works as long as poison and good food differ in some feature, or in some weighted mix of features. It fails
when what makes a bush poison is a *combination*. Here a bush is poison when its two colour features are both high
or both low, and good when one is high and the other low. No weighting of the features can tell the two kinds
apart: whatever a lesson teaches about one poison, it teaches the opposite about the other.

This stage adds a new region in front of the learning, the **pallium**. It spreads the look of the bush ahead out
over many cells, few of them active at a time, so that every kind of bush gets cells of its own. A lesson then
lands on the cells of the bush that was eaten, and not on its look-alikes.

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="2.2"></div>

## The circuit

- **`pallium`**, 128 cells. Each reads the colour features of the eye that points straight ahead, through
  synapses with random strengths. The wiring is random and evolution does not shape it: what matters is that it
  is different for every cell, not what it is.
- **Few cells at a time.** Of the 128 cells only the two that receive the most input fire; the others are held
  silent. The brain does this with inhibitory cells that every active cell excites; the model takes the shortcut
  and keeps the strongest two (*k-winners-take-all*). Because so few cells fire, two kinds of bush that share most
  of their look still share almost none of their active cells.
- **The lesson.** Pain teaches the synapses from the pallium onto the aversive cells, by the same rule that has
  taught the synapses from the look since the association stage: what was active just before the pain is
  strengthened. The old route stays: the look itself still learns as before. Evolution sets how fast each route
  learns.

Only the eye ahead feeds the pallium. At a bite the side eyes see the neighbouring bushes, and whatever they see
would be taught as well. An animal turns to a bush before it bites it, so the eye ahead sees the one that counts.

From this stage on, how strongly the look inputs adapt (the habituation of chapter 1) is set by evolution too.

## The biology: the oldest cortex

The *pallium* is the roof of the forebrain of all vertebrates; in mammals most of it became the cerebral cortex.
Its oldest part is olfactory: the piriform cortex, where every cell receives input from a random handful of the
smell channels, and only a few percent of the cells respond to any one smell. Insects arrived at the same design
on their own, in the *mushroom body*: about fifty smell channels fan out onto thousands of Kenyon cells, of which a
few percent fire, held down by a single inhibitory cell that all of them excite. Such a random, sparse expansion
separates inputs that overlap, which is why a fly can learn to avoid one smell and not its look-alike.

Vision, too, identifies a thing best when it is looked at directly. A fish turns to its prey before it strikes;
many fish have a patch of the retina with denser cells for this. The eye ahead of this model stands for that.

That the first vertebrate pallium did this job for vision is a guess of the model; that it began as such a sensory
association region is not.

## The world: kinds that only a combination tells apart

The world of the affect stage, with one change: the four new kinds of bush in every life now have looks that lie
on the corners of a square. Two colour directions are drawn for every life; one poison is high in both, the other
low in both, and the two good kinds are high in one and low in the other. Which kinds are poison is drawn anew in
every life as well. The new kinds are also less alike than before, which makes up for the harder task.

## Results

How to read the table and the charts: see [How a stage is judged](index.qmd#sec-judged).

### Main against control

The control is the brain of the affect stage in this world: it learns from pain on the look alone.

<div data-life="curves" data-stage="2.2"></div>

<div data-life="summary" data-stage="2.2"></div>

When both populations live in one world together, the animals with a pallium come out ahead in every seed.
Re-evaluated apart, each among its own kind, they are ahead in two seeds of three. Over the generations of evolution
itself the two populations run about level.

### Is the circuit used?

<div data-life="lesions" data-stage="2.2"></div>

In one seed of three the pallium is used. There it carries all of the learning: switching learning off costs as
much as silencing the pallium, and the look's own learning has been turned down. In the other two seeds neither the
pallium nor learning as a whole costs anything in the world. The states of the affect stage are still used in every
seed.

What holds the lessons back in the world is not the pallium's code. Followed through a life, the cells that fire at
a bush the animal has learned about are mostly the cells that fired at its lesson, and hardly ever those of the
other kinds. But two things stand in the way.

- **A lesson saves little.** Pain already ends a visit to a poison bush after a bite or two, and the alarm of the
  affect stage carries the animal off after a few. What knowing the poison by its look can still save is the first
  bite at the next bush of that kind.
- **Evolution damps aversion close up.** In every population, evolution has given the inputs that see a bush right
  ahead synapses that hold the aversive cells down: approach what is in front of you. A lesson has to overcome that before it can stop a
  bite. Where the lessons cost more good food than they save, evolution damps them further, and it can do so through
  the learning rule itself, by making a lesson undo itself or erase the ones before.

### In the lab

One animal at a time, outside the world: it eats from four new bushes, two of each kind, twice, and is then shown
each bush again.

<div data-life="table" data-stage="2.2" data-example="xor_lab"></div>

Learning on the look alone lowers the bites at all four bushes alike: it cannot tell the kinds apart, so it makes the
animal shy of all of them. Learning through the pallium lowers the bites at the poison bushes and leaves the good
ones alone, clearly in two seeds. In the third, evolution has turned the pallium's learning down. What the pallium
does is what this stage set out to add; whether this world rewards it enough to keep it is the open point.
